draft.title: Spectra and stars
card: A hot, low-pressure gas gives off light only at certain wavelengths, seen as bright lines. Each element has its own pattern of lines.
When light with all wavelengths passes through a cooler gas, that gas absorbs the same wavelengths it would emit. This leaves dark lines in the spectrum.
A star's spectrum shows dark lines from the gases in its outer layers. Matching these lines to known patterns tells us which elements the star contains.
A star's colour shows its surface temperature. A hotter star has a shorter peak wavelength, so it looks bluer. A cooler star looks redder.
draft.remember: Lines identify the elements in a star. Colour shows how hot its surface is.

a.q: A star's spectrum has dark lines at the same wavelengths as the bright lines of hydrogen. What does this show?
opts: Hydrogen is present in the star's outer gases
Hydrogen is the hottest element in the star
The star is giving off only hydrogen light
The star has a surface temperature of zero
a.why: Gas absorbs the same wavelengths it would emit, so matching dark lines show that hydrogen is in the star's outer layers. The lines do not show that the star emits only hydrogen light, because the star gives off all wavelengths and the gas removes some.
a.clue: A gas absorbs the wavelengths it would emit.

b.q: Astronomers find that star X looks blue and star Y looks red. What can they conclude about the surface temperatures?
opts: Star X is hotter than star Y
Star Y is hotter than star X
Both stars have the same temperature
Star X is made of different elements to star Y
b.why: A hotter star has a shorter peak wavelength, so it looks bluer. Star X is blue, so it is hotter. Many people think red means hot, but a red star has a longer peak wavelength and is cooler.
b.clue: Hotter objects peak at shorter wavelengths.

a.best: Hydrogen is present in the star's outer gases

b.best: Star X is hotter than star Y
